value: of five insecticidal lamps, the one peaking at 363 nm was most effective for male trapping; males were caught at all five lamps and female captures were minimal
method: field light-trapping with five insecticidal lamps (L360, L365, L370, L380, L405) run side by side
conditions: Pingtan County, Fuzhou, Fujian, China; wavelength tests 26-28 June and 3-5 July 2018 and 4-6 June 2019; lamps hung at 2 m, about 50 m apart and randomly placed daily, on from 19:00 to 04:00; peak-emergence catch 2,902 males and 9 females in total (female:male 1:322); at peak emergence (4-6 June 2019) the lamps did not differ significantly in male catch (F = 2.593, df = 4, p = 0.101; L360 took 31.0% of males), in the 2018 late-peak trapping they did (F = 5.367, df = 4, p = 0.007; L360 39.5%); the Discussion calls L360 the 363 nm lamp, the Introduction lists 363, 365, 368, 378 and 439 nm, and the label-to-peak mapping for the rest is in Table 1 (an image, not read); no replicate count beyond the trapping nights; lamp spectra differ in more than peak wavelength, so this is a catch comparison, not a spectral sensitivity

value: 14.6% of non-ovipositing females were phototactic and 0.6% flew directly toward the lamp; egg-laying females showed none
method: indoor phototaxis tests with moths held in net cages 7.0 m from a 25 W L360 lamp in a darkened room
conditions: tests 28-31 May 2021; Test 1 used 44 males and 43 females, Test 2 used 89 males and 78 females, Test 3 used 30 egg-laying females and none responded (Results 3.4); Results 3.4: Test 1, 7 of 43 non-ovipositing females (16.3%) moved toward the lamp and none flew directly to it; Test 2, 1 of 78 flew directly to the lamp and 9 more moved toward it (12.8%); 14.6% is given as an average of the tests, and 0.6% matches the average of 0 of 43 and 1 of 78, so it is one female; males in the same tests averaged 57.7% responding and 33.3% (45 males) flying directly to the lamp; no statistical test compares the sexes; 25 W L360 lamp, dark room 7.2 x 6 x 3 m, lamp on 21:00 to 04:00

where: Results 3.2 (CO2-Gated Heat Seeking Assays); assay set-up from Materials and Methods 2.1 and 2.3
quote: The heat-seeking responses of both Cx. tarsalis and Cx. quinquefasciatus were contingent on exposure to CO2.
value: heat-seeking response (to a warm target at 30 to 50 degrees C) contingent on exposure to CO2
conditions: 6 to 10 day old mated females; YOLO strain (BEI Resources NR-43026), a laboratory colony the paper says was collected in Yolo County, California; eight replicates (n = 15) per condition per species (Figure 6 caption); Results 3.2: both species responded significantly more after 30,000 than after 2100 ppm CO2, and at 30,000 ppm the proportion heat-seeking rose with target temperature to a peak at 40 and 45 °C; at 30,000 ppm Cx. tarsalis responded significantly more than Cx. quinquefasciatus (Chisq 15.22, p < 0.01), while after 2100 ppm the two did not differ at 30 to 40 °C and Cx. quinquefasciatus responded significantly more at 45 and 50 °C; landing proportions are in Table 1 (not read here; main's Cx. territans row from this paper gives about 4 to 12%); the sentence for Cx. territans in the same paper (no response with or without CO2) is on main already
note: Licence: the MDPI page metadata lists CC BY 3.0 (WebFetch of www.mdpi.com/2075-4450/13/1/92). Both species share one quoted sentence; each record states the finding for its own species. Not a thermopreference value: the paper's Tp results for these species were not filed. Laboratory colonies of the wild species, not domestic breeds. Names: Culex tarsalis Coquillett and Culex quinquefasciatus Say as printed in the paper (abbreviated Cx. in the quote). The printed sentence ends with '(Table 1; Supplementary Tables S1 and S2)', omitted from the quote.
